extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (calculus/real analysis) and readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style chapter covering differentiability, mean value theorems, smooth/analytic functions, power series, and a construction of the Riemann integral. Intended as teaching/exposition material for undergraduates or advanced high-school students learning real analysis/calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of differentiability at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: Let U be an open subset of R and f:U→R. f is differentiable at p∈U if the limit lim_{h→0} (f(p+h)−f(p))/h exists; the value is denoted f'(p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational criterion: the derivative is the limit of secant slopes as h→0. If differentiable at p then f is continuous at p (Exercise 28.1.2). Note the convention that the fraction is considered as a function of h excluding h=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain requirement for derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivatives are defined for functions on open intervals (or open subsets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g. if f:[a,b]→R, the derivative f'(a) does not make sense since f is not defined on an open neighborhood of a. One may still define derivatives at interior points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum rule (differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g are differentiable on U then (f+g)'(x) = f'(x) + g'(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be interpreted pointwise: if f and g are differentiable at p then (f+g) is differentiable at p with derivative f'(p)+g'(p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product rule (differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g are differentiable on U then (f·g)'(x) = f'(x) g(x) + f(x) g'(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via rewriting the difference quotient and taking limits; the rule holds pointwise as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain rule (differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:U→V and g:V→R are differentiable, then (g∘f)'(x) = g'(f(x)) · f'(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful technical detail: when forming the quotient g(f(p+h))−g(q) over f(p+h)−q one must handle cases where denominator is zero; define auxiliary Q(y) to ensure continuity and then take limits (see exposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative of elementary functions (selected)
rubrics_metrics.description: exp'(x) = exp(x); sin' = cos; cos' = −sin; (log x)' = 1/x on R_{>0}; power rule (x^r)' = r x^{r−1} for r∈R on R_{>0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some formulas are used without full rigorous derivation at this stage; the power rule for real exponents uses exp/log and the chain rule. Domain restrictions (e.g. R_{>0}) are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of derivative as slope/tangent
rubrics_metrics.description: f'(p) represents the slope of the tangent line at (p,f(p)), the limit of secant slopes (f(p+h)−f(p))/h as h→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graphical intuition (secant lines approach tangent). This justifies viewing f' as describing instantaneous rates (with unit/interpretation caveats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local maximum/minimum definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A local maximum: p∈U such that ∃ open neighborhood V⊂U with f(p) ≥ f(x) for all x∈V. Local minimum defined similarly; local extrema means either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, local maximum of f is local minimum of −f. These definitions set up Fermat's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat's theorem on stationary points
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:U→R is differentiable and p∈U is a local extrema, then f'(p) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a necessary condition for interior extrema (not sufficient: critical points need not be extrema). Proof via contradiction using one-sided slopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using compactness to find global extrema
rubrics_metrics.description: To find global extrema on a possibly noncompact domain, restrict to a compact set Z, use differentiability to locate extrema in the interior S and check boundary points separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: optimize rectangle area with fixed perimeter by considering function on closed interval [0,10]; interior extremum found via derivative, endpoints checked manually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolle's theorem (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→R is continuous, differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), then ∃ c∈(a,b) with f'(c)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses existence of global max/min by compactness; is a special case of the Mean Value Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean value theorem (MVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→R is continuous and differentiable on (a,b), then ∃ c∈(a,b) such that f'(c) = (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: some tangent has same slope as the secant; proof reduces to Rolle's theorem by subtracting a linear function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racetrack principle (comparison via derivatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g:R→R differentiable with f(0)=g(0) and f'(x)≥g'(x) for every x>0 then f(x)≥g(x) for every x>0 (strict inequalities give strict conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses MVT on h=f−g: a negative value leads to a point where derivative sign contradicts hypothesis. Useful for monotonicity/integral comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio mean value theorem (Cauchy mean value)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g:[a,b]→R are continuous and differentiable on (a,b) and g(a)≠g(b), then ∃ c∈(a,b) with f'(c)(g(b)−g(a)) = g'(c)(f(b)−f(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via Rolle's theorem applied to an appropriate linear combination h(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of smooth functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f:U→R is smooth if it is infinitely differentiable: f^{(n)} exists for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smoothness does not imply analyticity; example given of a smooth non-analytic function with all derivatives zero at the origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A power series is ∑_{n=0}^∞ a_n z^n where a_n∈R and z is a variable. Interpreted as a function on inputs h by ∑ a_n h^n where convergence allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abuse of notation remark: treat power series both as sequences of coefficients and as real-valued functions on their disk of convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius of convergence (Cauchy-Hadamard)
rubrics_metrics.description: For power series ∑ a_n z^n, the radius of convergence R satisfies 1/R = lim sup_{n→∞} |a_n|^{1/n} (with conventions R=0 if RHS=∞, R=∞ if RHS=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cauchy-Hadamard theorem: series converges absolutely if |h|<R and diverges if |h|>R. Behavior at |h|=R is inconclusive and must be checked case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation term-by-term for power series
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x)=∑_{n≥0} a_n x^n has radius of convergence R>0, then all derivatives exist on (−R,R) and are given by termwise differentiation (e.g. f'(x)=∑_{n≥1} n a_n x^{n−1}), and these derived series also converge on (−R,R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, power series define smooth functions on their interval of convergence. Proof uses uniform convergence (omitted here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor coefficients formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(x)=∑_{n≥0} a_n x^n on radius R>0 then a_n = f^{(n)}(0)/n!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by taking derivatives termwise and setting x=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of analytic function (local power series representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: f:U→R is analytic at p∈U if ∃ open neighborhood V of p and a power series ∑ a_n (x−p)^n such that f(x)=∑ a_n (x−p)^n for all x∈V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic ⇒ smooth. Having Taylor series with positive radius that actually converges to f on (p−R,p+R) implies f is analytic on that interval (Proposition 29.4.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure properties of analytic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums, products, compositions, and nonzero quotients of analytic functions are analytic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore most usual functions formed from analytic building blocks remain analytic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and properties of exp and log
rubrics_metrics.description: Define exp(x)=∑_{n≥0} x^n/n! (radius ∞) and e=exp(1). Then exp' = exp, exp(x+y)=exp(x)exp(y), exp(x)>0 for all x, exp is strictly increasing, and log is defined as inverse of exp with derivative 1/x on R_{>0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use power series properties and racetrack principle for monotonicity; these give a rigorous way to define exponentiation a^r := exp(r log a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex extension remark
rubrics_metrics.description: All the power series and analytic function results carry over to complex numbers (an∈C). Notably, if f:C→C is differentiable (in complex sense) then f is analytic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This points to stronger consequences in complex analysis; for real analysis the analogous implication does not hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending uniformly continuous functions (metric-space criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a metric space, N a complete metric space, and S a dense subspace of M. If ψ:S→N is uniformly continuous then there exists a unique continuous extension eψ:M→N such that eψ|_S = ψ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses Cauchy sequences: approximate each x∈M by x_n∈S, show ψ(x_n) is Cauchy using uniform continuity and completeness of N to define eψ(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann integral construction via rectangle functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define R([a,b]) as rectangle (step) functions, C0([a,b]) continuous functions, M([a,b]) = C0∪R. Define Σ: R([a,b])→R by summing rectangle areas. With metric d(f,g)=sup_{x∈[a,b]} |f(x)−g(x)|, R([a,b]) is dense in M([a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Σ is uniformly continuous and R is complete, there exists a unique continuous map ∫_a^b : M([a,b])→R extending Σ. This gives the Riemann integral for continuous (and rectangle) functions.
